title: Combat Lifesaver Extended Care
summary: What to do when a casualty has had initial trauma care but evacuation is delayed for hours: reassessment cycles, tourniquet checks, pain relief, wound care, fluids, warmth, and handoff. Updated to the May 2026 CoTCCC guidelines; no prescription dosing.

steps.title: Set a reassessment rhythm
steps.body: Extended care starts where MARCH ends (medical-001). Reassess at least every 15 minutes for a seriously hurt casualty, and after every move. Go in order: bleeding (tourniquets, packing, dressings), airway (position, secretions), breathing (rate, effort, chest seal), circulation (wrist pulse, skin color, temperature), alertness using AVPU - Alert, responds to Voice, responds only to Pain, Unresponsive - and body warmth. Any drop in alertness, a weaker pulse, or faster breathing is a warning. Write every check down with the time; the trend matters more than any single number.

steps.title: Recheck and, if trained, convert tourniquets
steps.body: At each check, look at every tourniquet: is it still tight, is the wound still dry, and is it still needed? The 2026 CoTCCC guidelines expect trained responders to try converting a tourniquet to a pressure or hemostatic dressing within about 2 hours, but only when the casualty is not in shock, the wound can be watched closely, and the limb is not amputated. Combat Lifesavers and other non-medics should not convert after 2 hours without medical direction, and a tourniquet on for more than 6 hours should stay on until the casualty reaches care with monitoring and lab support. Write down every application, loosening, conversion, and removal time.

steps.title: Manage pain safely
steps.body: Pain relief matters - severe pain raises stress, heart rate, and breathing rate. For a layperson, use over-the-counter pain medicine and follow the label exactly. Acetaminophen does not affect clotting and is generally the safest choice after trauma. Do not give aspirin to an injured or bleeding person. Ask a clinician before giving ibuprofen or similar drugs to someone who is bleeding, may need surgery, or has kidney problems. Splinting, padding, warmth, and calm reassurance also reduce pain. Strong prescription pain medicines and ketamine are given only by trained, authorized medics; do not give alcohol or sedatives.

steps.title: Shift from bleeding control to wound care
steps.body: Once bleeding is controlled and stable, prevent infection (see medical-024). Leave hemostatic packing in place. For other wounds, irrigate with drinkable water - at least 1 quart (1 L), using a squeeze bottle or a bag with a pinhole for good pressure. Do not add iodine, peroxide, or soap to the irrigation water. Leave contaminated wounds, bites, punctures, and gunshot wounds open under a clean dressing rather than closing them. Change dressings at least daily or when soaked. Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks, or fever mean infection - antibiotics are a prescription decision, so get medical help or advice as fast as you can.

steps.title: Fluids, food, and urine
steps.body: A casualty who is fully awake, can swallow, is not vomiting, and has no belly wound can take small, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration solution (medical-008), especially if evacuation is many hours away. Do not give anything by mouth to someone who is drowsy, confused, or vomiting. Watch urine: pale yellow is good; dark urine or no urine for many hours suggests dehydration or worsening shock. IV and blood transfusions are only for trained medics - the current guidelines prefer whole blood, and aim for a returning wrist pulse and better alertness rather than normal blood pressure.

steps.title: Prevent hypothermia and pressure injuries
steps.body: Injured people chill quickly even indoors. Keep the casualty insulated from the ground, out of wind and rain, in dry clothing, and wrapped in a sleeping bag or blankets with a windproof outer layer. The TCCC guidelines place active heat (such as a heating blanket) on the front of the torso and under the arms, never directly against the skin. Every 2 hours or so, help an immobile casualty shift position and pad bony points to avoid pressure sores. Help them urinate into a bottle so they do not lie in wet clothing.

steps.title: Package for evacuation and hand off
steps.body: Before moving the casualty, recheck every tourniquet, dressing, and seal. Wrap them for warmth, secure them to a litter, and pad under the knees and around the head. Rigid neck collars and backboards are no longer required for spinal protection; pad and limit motion instead (medical-021). Prepare a MIST report: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs (latest vitals and trends), Treatments with times, including all medicines, allergies, and tourniquet times. Send your written notes, or a DD Form 1380 card, with the casualty. Keep watching the airway during the move.

warnings: Extended care needs hands-on training - take a Combat Lifesaver, Wilderness First Responder, or similar course before you need it.
Tourniquet conversion can restart deadly bleeding. Only trained responders should try it, within the limits above.
This guide gives no prescription drug doses. Antibiotics, ketamine, opioids, TXA, and IV fluids require a trained, authorized provider.
proTips: Write 'TQ' plus the time on the casualty's forehead or on tape on the tourniquet so the time is never lost.
Use a simple vitals log: time, pulse, breathing rate, AVPU, skin, notes. One line every 15 minutes.
Practice reciting a MIST report out loud; it should take under a minute.
source: CoTCCC TCCC Guidelines (May 2026) / U.S. Army Combat Lifesaver / WMS

whenNotTo: Do not convert a tourniquet if the casualty is in shock, the limb is amputated, you cannot watch the wound, or it has been on more than 6 hours.
Do not close contaminated wounds, bites, or punctures in the field.
Do not give anything by mouth to a drowsy, confused, vomiting, or belly-wounded casualty.

quickGlance.situation: A casualty has had initial trauma care, but evacuation is delayed for hours.
immediate: Reassess every 15 minutes: bleeding, airway, breathing, pulse, AVPU, warmth
Check every tourniquet; only trained responders convert, within about 2 hours
Keep the casualty insulated, dry, and wrapped
then: Irrigate and dress wounds; give OTC pain medicine by the label (no aspirin)
Prepare a MIST report and send written notes with the casualty
